title: Scholastics dispute whether unformed faith is a virtue: name-fight, not thing-fight
source_text: XI. An autem fides informis sit virtus, inter se disputant Doctores Scholastici. Virtutem esse negat Thomas. Alii vero ut Durandus & Bonaventura simpliciter affirmant fidem etiam mortuam & informem esse virtutem. Sed inter eos est de nomine certamen. Etenim qui affirmant mortuam istam fidem virtutem, virtutem esse sumunt sensu generali, prout describitur habitus animi rectae rationi consentaneus, idemque inclinans ad actum legi divinae consentaneum. Quo sensu in Schola Romana nemo negat fidem informem virtutem dici posse. Quae quantumlibet informis sit, manet semper juxta eos, habitus, quo intellectus voluntatis imperio captivatus in obsequium fidei firmiter ea credit quae divinitus credenda praecipiuntur. Qui vero negant fidem informem esse virtutem, virtutis nomen restringunt ad illam qua recte vivitur, & quae simpliciter bonum facit habentem. Juxta eam acceptionem concedunt omnes nec fidem, nec ullum habitum moraliter bonum, seclusa charitate virtutem esse; ut docet Estius ad distinctionem 23. lib. 3. Sentent. paragr. 9.
pass_a_gloss: But whether unformed faith is a virtue, the Scholastic Doctors dispute among themselves. Thomas denies that it is a virtue. Others, however, such as Durandus and Bonaventure simply affirm that even dead and unformed faith is a virtue. But among them there is a contest about the name. For those who affirm that dead faith is a virtue take virtue in a general sense, as it is described as a habit of the mind agreeing with right reason, and likewise inclining to an act agreeing with the divine law. In which sense in the Roman School no one denies that unformed faith can be called a virtue. Which, however unformed it may be, always remains according to them a habit by which the intellect, captivated by the command of the will into the obedience of faith, firmly believes those things which are divinely commanded to be believed. But those who deny that unformed faith is a virtue restrict the name of virtue to that by which one lives rightly, and which simply makes its possessor good. According to that acceptance all concede that neither faith nor any morally good habit, charity being shut out, is a virtue; as Estius teaches on distinction 23 of book 3 of the Sentences, paragraph 9.
pass_b_english: Scholastics split on whether unformed faith is a virtue: Thomas says no; Durandus and Bonaventure say even dead faith is a virtue — but the fight is largely about the name.
Affirmers take virtue generally as a habit of mind agreeing with right reason and divine law; in that sense Rome does not deny unformed faith is a virtue, binding the intellect in obedience of faith.
Deniers reserve virtue for what makes one live rightly and simply good; on that sense all concede that without charity neither faith nor any morally good habit is a virtue.

lemmas.gloss: a habit of the mind agreeing with right reason

choices.why: Le Blanc frames the virtus dispute as verbal.
